content.text: I'll look at the project structure first to ground the plan in how this codebase actually works.

content.content:
# tsuzuri

A personal blog: a portrait and bio on the home page, and posts underneath.
Each post can carry more than one translation, and a reader is served
whichever translation best matches the locales their browser sends.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
```

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`           | Serves the site locally with hot reload.                   |
| `npm run build`         | Builds the production bundle.                              |
| `npm run start`         | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                |
| `npm run format`        | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.          |
| `npm run format:check`  | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.       |
| `npm run lint`          | Lints the whole project; also checks formatting.           |
| `npm run typecheck`     | Type-checks the project. The test runner compiles without checking types, so this is the only thing that does. |
| `npm test`              | Runs the unit test suite.                                  |
| `npm run test:e2e`      | Runs the end-to-end suite. Builds the app and serves it first, so it needs a browser — `npx playwright install chromium` once per machine. |

## Layout

- `app/(site)/` — the reader-facing route group: the home page, the post
  detail page, and the small data module they both read from.
- `shared/` — code shared by more than one part of the app, independent of any
  one route. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is the locale-fallback logic a
  post detail page calls into; `shared/blog-post-slug.ts` is the slug shape
  every post's `slug` is validated against.
- `shared/*.spec.ts` — unit tests, colocated with the code they cover.
- `e2e/` — end-to-end specs, kept apart from the unit tests above because they
  exercise the whole running app rather than one module in isolation.
- `docs/` — operational notes that do not belong in code comments, such as
  [deployment](docs/deployment.md).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Contributing

Changes go through a pull request rather than landing straight on `main`.
Before writing code, sketch the plan and get it approved — this catches a
misunderstood requirement while it is still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the checks
above pass.

# Deployment

Operational notes for running this site outside a local checkout. `npm run
build` produces what is served and `npm run start` serves it; everything below
is what a real deployment target adds around that pair.

## Environments

| Environment | Trigger                     | Notes                            |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Production  | Push to `main`              | Serves the default locale first. |
| Preview     | Pull request opened/updated | One preview per pull request.    |

## Locale fallback

A reader's accepted locales come from their browser's `Accept-Language`
header. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is what turns that preference list
into the translation a post detail page renders — see its own documentation
for the exact resolution order. Deployment does not change that order; it only
changes which posts and translations the deployed build carries.

## Rolling back

Redeploy the previous commit's build. There is no database to migrate back —
the post catalog and everything else the app reads live in the build itself —
so a rollback here is just a redeploy.
---
{
	"name": "tsuzuri",
	"version": "0.1.0",
	"private": true,
	"type": "module",
	"engines": {
		"node": "22"
	},
	"scripts": {
		"dev": "next dev",
		"build": "next build",
		"start": "next start",
		"format": "biome format --write .",
		"format:check": "biome format .",
		"lint": "biome check .",
		"test": "jest --config jest.config.cjs",
		"test:e2e": "playwright test",
		"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
	},
	"dependencies": {
		"next": "^16.3.0",
		"react": "^19.2.0",
		"react-dom": "^19.2.0",
		"zod": "^4.3.6"
	},
	"devDependencies": {
		"@biomejs/biome": "^2.4.4",
		"@jest/globals": "^30.4.1",
		"@playwright/test": "^1.62.1",
		"@types/react": "^19.2.2",
		"jest": "^30.4.2",
		"typescript": "^5.9.3"
	}
}
---

content.text:
## Reader corrections — plan

### What a reader sees

A small form at the bottom of the post article, below the body, inside the existing `<article>` in `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/page.tsx`. Fields:

- **Correction** (required, plain text, short — cap around 1,000 characters so this stays "a typo, a broken link," not a full rewrite request).
- **Contact** (optional email, so the author can follow up or ask a clarifying question).
- A hidden honeypot field (see Abuse prevention).

On submit, the form replaces itself with a thank-you message; on validation failure it shows the specific problem inline. No page navigation — a client component wrapping a server action.

The form should record *which translation the reader was looking at* (locale + slug) without asking them to specify it — that's already known server-side from the resolved translation, so it just rides along as a hidden value. A correction on the `ja-JP` copy and one on the `en-US` copy of the same post are different things to act on.

### Submission flow

1. Reader fills the form, submits.
2. A server action (colocated with the page, e.g. `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/submit-correction.ts`) validates the payload with a `zod` schema — bounded correction length, optional email format, slug re-validated against `PostSlug` from `shared/blog-post-slug.ts`, locale re-validated against the post's actual translations (reject a locale that doesn't exist on that post, since it didn't come from a `<select>` the reader controlled).
3. On success, the action delivers the correction (see below) and returns an ok/error result the form renders.

### Where corrections go

This is the one real infrastructure decision here, so I want to be explicit about it. `docs/deployment.md` currently says outright: *"There is no database to migrate back — the post catalog and everything else the app reads live in the build itself."* Adding a database purely to store correction submissions would be a bigger architectural shift than the feature warrants for a single-author blog.

**Recommendation: email the author.** The server action sends the correction (text, slug, locale, optional reader contact) via a transactional email API (e.g. Resend, which has a generous free tier and a minimal SDK) to an address set via an environment variable. Nothing is persisted in the app at all — no database, no admin UI, no new route group, consistent with the "no API surface yet" note in `app/(site)/layout.tsx`. The author triages corrections in their inbox and edits `posts-data.ts` by hand, the same way every other post edit happens today.

Alternatives considered and set aside for now:
- **A real database** — the natural place to grow into if correction volume ever justifies a moderation queue, but disproportionate for launch; would also be the first thing in this codebase to break the "rollback = redeploy" story in `docs/deployment.md`.
- **Auto-file a GitHub issue** — appealing since posts are already in git, but ties the feature to this repo specifically living on GitHub and needs a bot token with issue-write scope; more moving parts than email for the same outcome.
- **Plain `mailto:` link, no form/server action at all** — the zero-infrastructure option. Rejected because it hands the reader off to their own mail client rather than a short in-page action, which is what was asked for.

Needs one new secret (email API key) and one new env var (destination address) — worth flagging since that's ops work beyond this PR's diff, likely a `docs/` note alongside the existing deployment doc.

### Abuse prevention

No accounts, no captcha for v1 — matches the site's current lack of any auth/API surface. Instead:
- A hidden honeypot field; anything that fills it is silently dropped.
- Length caps enforced by the zod schema (already needed for validation anyway).
- Basic rate limiting is hard to do well without state to track it in — deferred; if spam becomes real, that's the trigger to revisit the "no database" call above, not to bolt on an ad hoc counter now.

### Where the code lives

Per `AGENTS.md`, this is entirely one route's concern, so it's colocated under `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/`, not `shared/`:
- `correction-form.tsx` — the client component.
- `submit-correction.ts` — the server action + zod schema.
- `submit-correction.spec.ts` — unit tests for validation (bad locale, oversized text, honeypot filled, malformed email).

Nothing here is a second call site for existing `shared/` code beyond re-validating against `PostSlug` and the post's own `translations`, which already live there.

### Testing

- Unit: schema validation edge cases (empty, too long, unknown locale, honeypot).
- E2E (`e2e/`): happy path (submit → thank-you message) and one rejected case (empty submission → inline error), with the email call mocked/stubbed so the suite doesn't hit a real provider.

### Non-goals for v1

- No moderation queue or admin view of submitted corrections.
- No diff/suggestion UI (reader isn't proposing exact replacement text, just describing the problem).
- No captcha/rate-limit infra beyond the honeypot.

### Open item before implementation starts

The email-provider choice and the new secret/env var are the part most worth a second look — that's infrastructure this repo doesn't have today. Everything else above I'd consider ready to turn into a PR plan once that's confirmed.
